nameStory: Aglantha digitale gets its scientific name from the Greek word 'aglantha' meaning 'bright' or 'shining,' referring to its translucent, glass-like appearance that seems to glow in the water. The species name 'digitale' comes from Latin meaning 'finger-like,' likely describing the shape of its bell or tentacles.
description: Aglantha digitale is a small, translucent jellyfish that drifts through New England's cold coastal waters. This hydrozoan has a bell-shaped body that pulses gently as it moves through the water column. It's one of the most common jellyfish in Arctic and sub-Arctic waters, occasionally appearing in our northern New England coastal areas. Like other hydrozoans, it has a simpler body structure than the larger, more familiar jellyfish most people know.

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Exhibits a distinctive two-speed swimming pattern - normally pulses its bell slowly and gracefully, but can suddenly dart away with rapid, jerky movements when startled

idTips.label: Bell shape
idTips.description: Has a rounded, dome-like bell that appears crystal clear and glass-like when viewed in water

idTips.label: Transparency
idTips.description: Body is so translucent it's almost invisible, with internal structures faintly visible like shadows within glass

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to easily fit within a cupped hand, much smaller than the dinner-plate sized moon jellies commonly seen

idTips.label: Water preference
idTips.description: Found in cold water that feels shockingly frigid to the touch, typically in deeper areas rather than warm tidal pools

habitat: Found in the cold coastal waters of northern New England, particularly in deeper waters offshore rather than in shallow tidal areas. This Arctic species occasionally drifts into our region during cooler periods, typically in areas with strong cold-water currents. Most likely encountered in the Gulf of Maine's deeper waters rather than close to shore.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing in northern New England waters as Arctic currents bring them south during late spring cold snaps.
seasonality.summer: Most likely to be observed during cooler summer periods when cold-water upwelling occurs along the coast.
seasonality.fall: Can persist into early fall in deeper, consistently cold waters before retreating northward.
seasonality.winter: Rarely observed due to harsh weather conditions making marine observation difficult, though they may be present in deep waters.

funFact: This jellyfish has a built-in 'panic button' - it can instantly switch from peaceful drifting to lightning-fast escape swimming, like a underwater sports car that suddenly shifts from cruise control to race mode!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, translucent jellyfish, but the unique dual swimming behavior sets it apart - if you see a small clear jellyfish that suddenly rockets away when disturbed, you've likely found Aglantha digitale. Remember: 'Aglantha has attitude' - it's the one that darts away dramatically.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents the southern edge of Arctic marine life occasionally visiting New England waters. Hydrozoans like Aglantha are often called 'true jellyfish' but are actually more closely related to coral and sea anemones than to the larger scyphozoan jellies most people know.
compareHints: As the only Aglantha species in New England waters, it's best compared to other small hydrozoans in the region. Unlike most other small jellyfish that maintain consistent swimming speeds, Aglantha's dramatic speed changes make it unique. Most similar small jellies lack this distinctive dual-speed swimming behavior and tend to be more consistent in their movements.
